claims.text: Solutionized near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be prepared as a homogenized, single-phase solid solution free of significant precipitates or ordering.
The absence of substantial second-phase particles or ordering features leaves dislocations with minimal barriers to glide.
Plastic deformation in single-phase near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi proceeds primarily through relatively unhindered dislocation motion.
Relatively unhindered dislocation motion produces insufficient work hardening.
Insufficient work hardening causes the low hardness and strength of the alloy.
At high temperature, deformation is mainly controlled by dislocations.
Dislocation morphology and density control the mechanical properties of the alloy.
Insufficient short-range ordering fails to create significant barriers to dislocation motion.
The lack of stable secondary phases fails to create significant barriers to dislocation motion.
The low-obstacle microstructure leads to extensive planar slip.
The low-obstacle microstructure leads to limited strain hardening.
Higher strain rates and lower temperatures will produce predominantly planar dislocation glide.
Higher strain rates and lower temperatures will produce limited deformation twinning.
Higher strain rates and lower temperatures will produce limited deformation-induced phase transformation.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has lower hardness and yield strength than precipitation-hardened or ordered CoCrFeNiTi variants.
At room temperature and low strain rate, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi typically has a hardness of 130–250 HV.
At room temperature and low strain rate, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi typically has a yield strength below approximately 400 MPa.
The room-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation of single-phase CoCrFeNiTi is driven mainly by dislocation flow in a simple matrix.
Introducing precipitates or promoting ordering may change the deformation mechanism and mechanical response.
Direct data for the stacking-fault energy and short-range ordering of CoCrFeNiTi are limited.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly restricted to material without significant precipitates or ordering, yet detecting precipitates or ordering is treated as falsification. Such detection would instead show that the prepared sample falls outside the stated initial-state and boundary conditions.
